office_does: State Representatives write and vote on state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets; each district elects two to two-year terms.
race_blurb: One-term Democratic Representative Adison Richards faces Republican David Olson, a 13-year Peninsula School Board member who led the primary. They differ most on reproductive and gender policy and spending; both opposed the 2025 B&O tax package. On parental rights, Olson campaigns on parents' right to be informed, while Richards voted for ESHB 1296 after voting for twelve floor amendments, most of which failed, that would have added to or restored parent rights in it.

candidates.summary: Peninsula School Board member since 2013, retired Navy officer and former public finance banker, running on lower spending, no new taxes, housing supply and parental rights.
highlights: Calls for 'no more broad-based taxes' and opposes the 2025 B&O tax package (HB 2081) [S2]
Would oppose rent caps like HB 1217 and cut red tape to build housing [S2]
Supports sex-based school sports and locker-room privacy [S2]
Would 'Defend parents' right to be informed and involved' in their child's education [S2]

taxes.basis: Criticizes passing an income tax, calls for no more broad-based taxes and votes against future tax increases.

spending.basis: Calls to reduce and cut wasteful spending and tie budgets to results.

housing.basis: Frames affordability as a supply and cost-to-build problem; opposes rent caps and supports permitting and zoning reform.

safety.basis: Calls to restore public safety and stand with law enforcement.

experience.basis: Thirteen years in elected school-board office but new to the Legislature, challenging a one-term incumbent.

local-control.basis: Calls himself a strong advocate for local control and would standardize permits with local control preserved.

social.basis: Would defend sex-based sports and locker-room privacy.

parental-rights.basis: Supports parents' right to be informed, access to curriculum information, and pushing back on policies that cut parents out of decisions.

candidates.summary: Attorney and one-term state representative, running on affordability, police funding, trades education and reproductive rights.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 (2026 tax on millionaires) and the major 2025 revenue bills [S5][S10][S11]
Sponsored legislation to fund more local police officers, per his campaign [S1][S3]
Pledges to protect reproductive freedom; endorsed by Planned Parenthood and Pro-Choice Washington [S3][S4]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list, after voting yea on all twelve recorded floor amendments to add or restore parent rights; ten failed [S6][S7]

taxes.basis: Voted nay on ESSB 6346 and the 2025 gas, B&O, capital gains/estate and services tax bills, while saying tax fairness requires 'more than simply raising taxes on the wealthy'.

spending.basis: Seeks dedicated pre-K and technical-school funding alongside 'more accountability and efficiency'.

housing.basis: Attributes rising prices largely to low supply and wants it made easier to build, especially in urban cores.

safety.basis: Sponsored bills to fund more police officers and raise sexual-assault penalties.

climate.basis: Wants to expand clean energy careers and diversify energy sources.

immigration.basis: Says he voted to ban law enforcement, including ICE, from wearing face masks.

healthcare.basis: Supports more competition among hospitals and providers while fighting federal cuts.

social.basis: Pledges to protect reproductive freedom and says government should stay out of 'who we love, or who we are'; endorsed by Planned Parenthood and Pro-Choice Washington.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296's amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no further statements found.
